value.overview: The Streak-crowned Antvireo is a small, secretive antbird of humid forests in Central America. It spends most of its time in dense vegetation from the understory to the lower mid-storey, where it searches for insects and other arthropods. Its contrasting crown streaks and quiet, deliberate movements can make it rewarding but challenging to find. Costa Rica forms an important part of its range, especially in lowland and foothill forest on the Caribbean side and in suitable northern habitats.
value.classification: The Streak-crowned Antvireo belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the genus Dysithamnus. It is considered a monotypic species, with no widely recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This compact antbird has a short tail and a relatively stout, slightly hooked bill. The male has a dark gray head and upperparts, with conspicuous pale streaking across the crown and nape, contrasting with paler underparts. Females are generally browner and more subdued, but also show the characteristic streaked crown pattern. It is usually detected by movement or song in tangled understory vegetation rather than by prolonged, exposed views.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from extreme southeastern Honduras through Nicaragua and across much of Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid evergreen forest on the Caribbean slope, as well as some northern areas and foothill sites, generally from sea level to about 800 meters. It favors primary and mature forest with dense understory and can occur less frequently in mature secondary woodland. It is regularly associated with forested reserves and connected foothill habitats.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. In Costa Rica, individuals are expected to remain in suitable forest habitats throughout the year, although local movements may occur when birds follow food resources or shift through their territories.
value.breeding: Reliable detailed information on the breeding biology of the Streak-crowned Antvireo is limited. Like related antvireos, it is believed to form territorial pairs and to place a small nest in dense vegetation, where both adults contribute to incubation and care of the young. Breeding activity is likely linked to local rainfall and food availability, but the timing and nest characteristics for this species are not sufficiently documented here to describe confidently.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, including spiders and likely a variety of larvae and beetles. The bird searches methodically through leaves, twigs, vines, and dense shrubs in the lower forest layers. It may forage alone, in pairs, or as part of mixed-species understory flocks. It is not dependent on army-ant swarms, although it can take advantage of insects disturbed by other animals.
value.behavior: The Streak-crowned Antvireo is usually quiet, wary, and difficult to observe in thick vegetation. It moves by short hops between branches and foliage, pausing frequently while inspecting leaves for prey. Pairs maintain territories and may respond to vocal playback or neighboring birds. In Costa Rica it is sometimes encountered in mixed-species flocks, particularly in humid foothill forest, but it generally remains within the shaded understory and lower mid-storey.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified; available summaries generally describe the species as not currently facing a major range-wide decline.
